title: Trump: Senate Republicans agree that Donald Trump won by colluding with Russia
description_short: Trump: Senate Republicans agree that Donald Trump won by colluding with Russia
description_medium: On August 18, 2020, the Republican-controlled Senate Intelligence Committee released a report on Russian interference in the 2016 election. TrumpFile says the report described campaign contacts with Russian officials and shared polling data, but its headline goes further by saying Republicans agreed Trump won through collusion. That characterization is editorial framing, not a neutral statement of the committee’s conclusion.
description_long: On August 18, 2020, the Republican-led Senate Intelligence Committee issued the fifth volume of its investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election. TrumpFile’s account characterizes the report as confirming that Trump’s campaign accepted Russian offers of help, maintained contacts with Russian government officials, shared polling information and coordinated release timing of stolen information intended to hurt Hillary Clinton. The page presents those points as evidence that Republicans had accepted a collusion account, but “won by colluding” is its editorial framing, not a neutral summary of the report. The article identifies a 966-page Senate report and links its fifth volume, as well as a New York Times opinion piece. This record can describe the committee report and TrumpFile’s interpretation; it cannot infer from that framing alone that the committee found Trump won because of collusion. The title should be revised to identify the report and distinguish its findings from the article’s interpretation.
organization_tags: U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Senate Republicans agree that Donald Trump won by colluding with Russia
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Senate Republicans agree that Donald Trump won by colluding with Russia

notes: I read the linked TrumpFile timeline. It describes the Senate report’s findings and links Volume 5, but the headline’s claim that Republicans agreed Trump won through collusion is the timeline’s interpretation, not a neutral committee finding established by the supplied excerpt. Proposed correction: title this as the Senate report’s findings on Russian interference and campaign contacts.
proposed_correction: Senate Report Details Russian Interference and Trump Campaign Contacts

title: Trump's Intelligence director releases Russian disinformation on the public
description_short: Trump's Intelligence director releases Russian disinformation on the public
description_medium: On September 29, 2020, Director of National Intelligence John Ratcliffe declassified a Russian intelligence allegation about Hillary Clinton and sent it to Senate Judiciary Chairman Lindsey Graham. The TrumpFile account says the Senate Intelligence Committee had already rejected the claim during its bipartisan inquiry. Democrats and former intelligence officials objected that releasing it could amplify unsubstantiated Russian material during the campaign.
description_long: On September 29, 2020, Director of National Intelligence John Ratcliffe declassified and sent a Russian intelligence assessment to Senate Judiciary Chairman Lindsey Graham. It alleged Hillary Clinton was personally behind an effort to tie Donald Trump to Vladimir Putin and Russia’s hacking of Democratic National Committee material. The TrumpFile account says the Senate Intelligence Committee had already considered and rejected the allegation during its bipartisan inquiry into Russian election interference. Democrats objected that the disclosure placed a discredited foreign-intelligence claim into public debate and could reinforce Trump’s claims about the investigation. The page also reports criticism from former senior intelligence officials. The event was Ratcliffe’s decision to disclose the assessment; the allegation itself was not established as fact. The source records disagreement about whether the release served public oversight or amplified Russian disinformation during the 2020 campaign.

title: Trump: Adviser: 20 states might help overturn the election for Trump
description_short: Trump: Adviser: 20 states might help overturn the election for Trump
description_medium: After the 2020 election, journalist Laurie Garrett reported that a senior Trump adviser said the campaign was trying to persuade electors in 20 states to vote for Trump despite the results. The TrumpFile timeline contrasts her report with a separate adviser’s denial to The New York Times. The sources document conflicting accounts, not commitments by electors or a verified operation in twenty states.
description_long: After the 2020 election, journalist Laurie Garrett reported that a senior Trump adviser said the campaign was trying to persuade electors in 20 states to vote for Trump despite the results. The described mechanism was a faithless-elector effort: persuading state-selected electors to cast their votes for a different candidate. The TrumpFile timeline juxtaposes Garrett’s report with a New York Times account from the previous day in which another adviser dismissed the possibility and said Trump knew the election was over. The sources therefore document conflicting accounts attributed to unnamed advisers, not commitments by electors or a verified operation in twenty states. The page situates the report among efforts to find a way for Trump to remain in office after the election. It does not name the adviser or states, or provide evidence that any elector agreed. This is a report of a proposed effort, not proof it occurred or changed the outcome.

title: Trump: Stop The Steal organizer says he's working with congressmen for ‘war' at Capitol
description_short: Trump: Stop The Steal organizer says he's working with congressmen for ‘war' at Capitol
description_medium: Stop the Steal organizer Ali Alexander said in a livestream that he and Representatives Paul Gosar, Mo Brooks and Andy Biggs planned a “loud war” to pressure Congress during the January 6 electoral count. The linked page attributes the account to Alexander and says the lawmakers denied knowing him. Its timeline dates the event December 28, while the record metadata says December 29.
description_long: On December 28, 2020, Stop the Steal organizer Ali Alexander said in a livestream that he had worked with Representatives Paul Gosar, Mo Brooks and Andy Biggs to plan pressure on Congress during the January 6 electoral vote count. He called the tactic a “loud war” and described its purpose as changing lawmakers’ minds from outside the Capitol. The TrumpFile account says Alexander founded Stop the Steal and had organized challenges at disputed ballot-counting sites. After the Capitol attack, it reports, Alexander was banned from Twitter and said he should not be blamed. The page also says the three lawmakers denied knowing him despite Alexander’s public statements about their connections, and notes that the Arizona Republican Party had praised him in now-deleted posts. These are the article’s reports and Alexander’s claims; they do not establish that the lawmakers conspired with him or that he coordinated the attack. The timeline date differs from the record date and needs reconciliation.
subcategory: Stop the Steal and January 6 congressional pressure campaign

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Stop The Steal organizer says he's working with congressmen for ‘war' at Capitol
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Stop The Steal organizer says he's working with congressmen for ‘war' at Capitol

notes: I read the linked TrumpFile page. It gives Alexander’s livestream account, names the three representatives, reports their denial, and describes Alexander’s prior election activity. The page labels the timeline event December 28, 2020, while this record’s date field is December 29; the linked Washington Post page timed out during retrieval. Proposed correction: reconcile the event date against the publication date, then title the item around Alexander’s attributed claim rather than Trump’s direct action.
proposed_correction: Stop the Steal Organizer Says He Planned January 6 Pressure Campaign with GOP Lawmakers

title: Trump releases video condemning violence and ‘censorship'
description_short: Trump releases video condemning violence and ‘censorship'
description_medium: On January 13, 2021, Donald Trump released a recorded address condemning violence and future demonstrations while criticizing what he called censorship. The TrumpFile account says Stephen Miller, White House Counsel Pat Cipollone and deputy Pat Philbin helped draft it. Trump did not mention Joe Biden, concede the election, discuss the inauguration or address his second impeachment.
description_long: On January 13, 2021, six days after the attack on the Capitol, Donald Trump released a recorded address condemning violence and future demonstrations. He also criticized what he called censorship, referring to social-media restrictions and broader limits on speech. The TrumpFile account says Stephen Miller, White House Counsel Pat Cipollone and deputy Pat Philbin helped craft the language. It notes what the video did not address: Trump did not mention President-elect Joe Biden, concede the election, discuss the coming inauguration or refer to his second impeachment. The linked CNN report describes unrest inside the White House after the attack and Trump’s focus on pardons and his political fallout; it provides context for the moment but does not alter what he said in the video. The entry concerns Trump’s January 13 public statement after the Capitol attack, including its condemnation of violence and its complaint about censorship. It should not be read as a concession or as a discussion of impeachment proceedings.

preserved_fields.description_short: Trump releases video condemning violence and ‘censorship'
